_meta.description: Deterministic, code-enforced architectural/ergonomic constraints per room_type x size bucket. Not GPT-generated — these are hard facts (clearances, thresholds, appliance logic) that must never be contradicted by AI-generated prose. GPT/enrichment layers may explain or stylize these, but may not override them.

hard_rules: No island or peninsula — under 10m² cannot absorb the ~105cm clearance an island requires on both sides.
Never place the stove flush in a corner with no landing counter beside it — keep a minimum 40cm clear counter on at least one side of the cooktop for pot handling.
Single-wall or galley layout only; an L-shape needs more corner depth than this footprint allows.
space_saving_tips: Stack the oven under the counter with a storage drawer above or below it instead of a separate base cabinet — reclaims roughly 40cm of floor-level storage.
Use a combined oven+microwave unit to save counter width rather than two separate appliances.
Wall-mounted rail systems for utensils and pans free up drawer space entirely.
avoid: Full-size refrigerator — use a slim or under-counter unit.
Upper cabinets on both walls in a galley layout — leave one wall open-shelving-only to avoid a tunnel feel.

hard_rules: Still no true island; a narrow rolling cart (under 60cm depth) is the ceiling, and only if it leaves 105cm of clear walkway.
The stove clearance rule still applies — minimum 40cm landing zone beside the cooktop.
If an L-shape is used, the inside corner needs a carousel or blind-corner pull-out, not a dead unusable corner.
space_saving_tips: Under-oven drawer for baking trays and pan lids is the single best space recovery move at this size.
A pull-out pantry unit (15–20cm wide) beside the fridge uses otherwise wasted gap space.
Open shelving above the counter reduces visual bulk versus stacked upper cabinets.
avoid: Double-basin sink — a single basin with an integrated drainer frees counter length.
Decorative backsplash tile that doesn't also serve as the counter-to-cabinet gap filler.

hard_rules: A slim peninsula (max 60cm depth, under 150cm length) becomes viable only if 105cm clearance is kept on the walkway side.
The work triangle (sink–stove–fridge) must stay under 6m combined leg length or the layout is inefficient regardless of square footage.
Size the ventilation hood to the cooktop width, not the room — undersized hoods are the most common compact-kitchen mistake.
space_saving_tips: Under-oven drawer remains a permanent default at this size, not just a small-kitchen fix.
Corner carousel unit if an L-shape corner exists.
Vertical divider slots next to the oven (trays and cutting boards stored upright) save more than a drawer would.
avoid: A full kitchen island — a peninsula is the ceiling until 18m²+.
Open shelving on more than one full wall — some closed storage is still needed for visual calm at this size.

hard_rules: A true island becomes possible here, but only at minimum 90×150cm with 105cm clearance maintained on every side.
If an island is added, it should take on at most one function (prep OR seating OR sink) — combining more than one on a small island creates congestion.
Keep the work triangle intact even with an island present; don't let it interrupt the sink–stove–fridge path.
space_saving_tips: A dedicated small dining nook (2–4 seats) can now be split off from the cooking zone with a rug or half-wall.
Under-oven drawer remains standard practice regardless of available space.
Deep drawers instead of cabinet doors for pots and pans reduce bending and reclaim corner reach.
avoid: An island larger than 150cm on this footprint — it will choke the walkway clearance.

hard_rules: The island can grow to 100×180cm and take on two functions (e.g. prep + casual seating) since the clearance budget allows it.
A distinct dining zone (4–6 seats) is appropriate and should be visually separated from the cook zone, not merged into one continuous surface.
A pantry zone (even a single tall cabinet run) becomes worth dedicating space to at this size.
space_saving_tips: Under-oven drawer plus a second drawer stack for small appliances keeps counters clear.
An appliance garage (roll-front cabinet) hides small appliances without eating into usable counter.
avoid: Leaving the extra square meterage as unassigned open floor — every zone should have a function or it reads as wasted space.

hard_rules: The island can be full-scale (120×240cm) and absorb prep, secondary sink, and seating — this is the only bracket where that combination doesn't create congestion.
A separate walk-in or butler's pantry is architecturally justified here.
Multiple work zones can coexist, but each still needs its own clear circulation lane — size doesn't remove the clearance rules, it just gives room to satisfy them.
space_saving_tips: Under-oven drawer and a full drawer bank for cookware remain the default even at this scale — big kitchens fail from poor internal organization just as often as small ones.
An appliance garage or dedicated coffee station keeps the large island's surface from becoming permanent clutter.
avoid: Treating the extra space as license to skip zoning — an unstructured 35m² kitchen creates more wasted motion than a well-organized 12m² one.

hard_rules: A full wardrobe, a desk, and the bed will not all fit — pick two as fixed and treat the third as fold-away or shared with another room.
Swing-door wardrobes need a 70–90cm clearance arc to open; at this size that arc alone can consume a functional corner — use sliding or bi-fold doors instead.
Bed size caps at a Double/Full — a Queen leaves under 60cm clearance on both sides, which fails the minimum walk clearance.
space_saving_tips: Wall-mounted floating nightstands instead of freestanding units reclaim floor area.
A bed frame with integrated drawer storage replaces a separate dresser entirely.
Over-door hooks and a slim vertical shelf beside the wardrobe use vertical space the floor plan can't offer.
avoid: A reading chair as a separate piece — fold this function into the bed with a wall-mounted reading light and a slim shelf instead.

hard_rules: Queen bed is the practical ceiling; a King requires more clearance than 12m² supports on both long sides.
Wardrobe depth must stay at 60cm max (standard hanging depth) — deeper eats into the walk path.
Sliding wardrobe doors remain the default; swing doors are only viable if the wardrobe sits on the wall opposite the bed with no crossing traffic.
space_saving_tips: Under-bed drawers absorb seasonal storage that would otherwise need a dresser.
A slim floating desk (40cm depth) can double as a vanity/console near natural light.
avoid: A full-length dresser at the foot of the bed — it narrows the walk path below the 60cm minimum.

hard_rules: Queen bed plus a compact wardrobe and one additional piece (desk OR reading chair, not both) is the realistic ceiling.
Maintain minimum 60cm clearance on both sides of the bed and 90cm in the primary walk path per Neufert circulation minimums.
space_saving_tips: A slim bench at the foot of the bed replaces a full reading chair while using less depth.
Corner wardrobe placement can free a usable strip along the adjacent wall for a desk.
avoid: Placing the wardrobe and desk on the same wall — it creates one congested zone instead of distributing function around the room.

hard_rules: Queen or King both work now, but King requires the room's shortest side to be at minimum 3.4m to keep clearances intact.
A genuine reading nook (chair + side table) is appropriate here and should sit away from the direct bed sightline per the Sage/Sovereign privacy protocols.
space_saving_tips: A walk-in-style wardrobe zone (open on one side, not a full closet room) is achievable without sacrificing the reading nook.
avoid: Wall-to-wall area rugs — a rug should define the bed zone, not the whole room, or it flattens the zoning logic.

hard_rules: King bed with full clearance on all sides, plus a dedicated seating or work zone, fits without compromise.
This is the first bracket where a proper walk-in wardrobe (not just a wardrobe zone) is architecturally justified.
space_saving_tips: Use the extra footprint to separate 'sleep' and 'dress/work' into distinct zones with a rug or low console rather than letting furniture drift toward the center.
avoid: Filling the extra space with more furniture instead of more clearance — the persona system rewards breathing room, not density.

hard_rules: A full suite layout (bed, seating, desk, walk-in wardrobe) can coexist, but each zone still needs its own clearance envelope — size doesn't waive the 60–90cm minimums, it just makes them easy to satisfy.
Consider whether the room genuinely needs every function, or whether splitting into 'bedroom' plus an adjacent dressing area serves the persona better.
space_saving_tips: A furniture-based zone divider (open bookshelf, bench-back console) keeps the room from reading as one oversized undifferentiated box.
avoid: A single oversized bed as the only anchor with everything else pushed to the walls — this creates a hollow, unresolved center.

hard_rules: No dining set — even a 2-seat table needs more room than a micro balcony can spare alongside a walkable path.
Furniture must be wall-mounted or foldable; nothing freestanding should occupy floor space when not in use.
space_saving_tips: Railing-mounted planter boxes replace floor planters entirely.
A single fold-down wall shelf serves as the only 'table' surface needed.
avoid: Floor-standing planters — the single most common balcony space mistake at this size.

hard_rules: A slim 2-seat bistro set is the ceiling, and only if it folds or stores away.
Keep a minimum 45cm clear path to the railing at all times.
space_saving_tips: Vertical/tiered planter walls instead of ground planters.
Foldable chairs stored against the wall when not hosting.
avoid: A permanent umbrella base — dead weight taking floor space year-round for occasional shade.

hard_rules: A fixed 2-seat table becomes viable without needing to fold, but a 4-seat set is still too much for this footprint.
space_saving_tips: Built-in bench seating along one rail with storage underneath is more efficient than freestanding chairs.
avoid: Mixing more than two furniture styles — visual clutter reads worse on a small balcony than indoors.

hard_rules: A proper 2–4 seat dining setup fits without folding requirements.
space_saving_tips: A corner bench with an integrated planter box combines seating and greenery in one footprint.
avoid: Leaving the balcony purely decorative when the occupancy answers indicate daily-use intent.

hard_rules: Distinct lounge and dining zones can coexist if furniture depth stays under 70cm per zone.
space_saving_tips: A weather-resistant storage bench doubles as extra seating during hosting.
avoid: Oversized furniture scaled for an indoor room — outdoor pieces should stay visually lighter even when the footprint allows more.

hard_rules: A full outdoor living setup (lounge + dining + planting zone) is justified, but each zone still needs its own circulation buffer, same as indoor rooms.
space_saving_tips: A pergola or shade structure becomes worth the footprint at this size, freeing the layout from needing a movable umbrella.
avoid: Under-using the space as one big open zone with no defined activities — it reads as unfinished rather than generous.

hard_rules: No sectional — depth alone (typically 95–100cm+) will not leave a walkable circulation lane.
TV must be wall-mounted, not on a console, to reclaim floor depth.
space_saving_tips: A nesting coffee table (smaller table stows under the larger one) instead of one fixed piece.
Floating shelves instead of a media console for AV storage.
avoid: An area rug sized for a bigger room — oversized rugs make a small living room look smaller, not larger.

hard_rules: A 2-seater sofa plus one accent chair is the ceiling — a 3-seater will not leave the 90cm circulation minimum.
space_saving_tips: A wall-mounted TV with a slim floating shelf below instead of a console.
An ottoman with storage doubles as coffee table and extra seating.
avoid: A bulky sectional 'just in case' — it will dominate every sightline in the room.

hard_rules: A 3-seater sofa plus one accent chair fits if floated 60cm off the rear wall per the persona's command-position standard.
space_saving_tips: A slim console (under 35cm depth) rather than a deep media unit.
avoid: Placing the sofa diagonally 'to open up' the room — ortho-axial alignment reads calmer and uses less footprint.

hard_rules: A full 3-seater plus 2 accent pieces and a proper media console are all viable within Neufert clearance minimums.
space_saving_tips: A defined rug boundary (200×160cm+) anchors the seating zone without adding furniture.
avoid: Pushing every piece against the walls 'to save space' — floating the primary seating reads as considered, not cramped.

hard_rules: An L-shaped sectional or two full sofas in a conversational-circle layout both work at this size.
space_saving_tips: A secondary reading zone can be split off from the main seating cluster with a rug or bookshelf-back divider.
avoid: One oversized sectional as the sole anchor — it under-uses the room's zoning potential.

hard_rules: Multiple seating zones (primary conversation circle + secondary reading/media nook) are appropriate and expected at this size.
space_saving_tips: Furniture-based zone dividers keep the room from reading as one undifferentiated hall.
avoid: Symmetric 'showroom' arrangements that ignore the actual traffic pattern between doors — layout should follow real circulation, not just visual balance.

hard_rules: A murphy bed or sofa-bed is mandatory — a permanent bed frame will not leave room for any living function.
Storage must be entirely vertical since floor footprint is fully committed to sleep plus one activity zone.
space_saving_tips: A fold-down wall desk doubles as counter space when closed.
Under-platform storage drawers if a platform bed base is used instead of a full murphy unit.
avoid: A coffee table and a desk as two separate pieces — combine them into one adjustable-height surface.

hard_rules: A low-profile platform bed with under-bed storage becomes viable, still paired with a compact fold-down or wall-mounted desk.
space_saving_tips: A slim bookshelf turned perpendicular to the wall acts as both storage and a soft room divider.
avoid: A full dining table — a wall-mounted drop-leaf serves the same function in a fraction of the footprint.

hard_rules: Distinct sleep and living zones become possible using a furniture-based divider (bookshelf back, low console) rather than a wall.
space_saving_tips: A daybed-style frame lets the 'bed zone' double as casual seating during the day.
avoid: A zone boundary that isn't reinforced by furniture — a rug alone won't read as a real division in a studio.

hard_rules: A full bed (not murphy-dependent) plus a proper desk and a compact living seating area all fit with a defined divider.
space_saving_tips: A tall open shelving unit as the room divider adds storage capacity while doubling as the zone boundary.
avoid: Treating the studio as one continuous room — even at this size, missing zoning is the most common studio complaint.

hard_rules: Three functional zones (sleep, work, living/social) can coexist if each keeps its own circulation buffer.
space_saving_tips: A half-height partition or furniture wall gives the sleep zone real privacy without a full renovation.
avoid: Spreading furniture evenly across the whole footprint 'to fill the space' — defined zones with real gaps read better than uniform density.

hard_rules: At this size a studio functions closer to a true one-bedroom in practice — zoning discipline still matters even though square footage no longer forces it.
space_saving_tips: A furniture-defined spine (console table run) between zones mimics the wayfinding a real hallway would give.
avoid: Under-using the extra space as one large open living area with the bed pushed to a corner — this reads as unfinished rather than intentionally large.

hard_rules: True open-plan function is difficult under 10m² — treat it as one unified zone rather than three sub-zones; don't force a kitchen island or a separate dining table into this footprint.
space_saving_tips: A single multi-function table serves as both prep-adjacent dining and work surface.
avoid: Attempting three distinct zones — pick two (e.g. cook+eat) and let the third borrow from an adjacent room if possible.

hard_rules: A drop-leaf or extendable dining table lets the zone flex between 2-seat daily use and 4-seat hosting without a permanent footprint commitment.
space_saving_tips: Define the kitchen edge with a half-height counter instead of full uppers, keeping sightlines open across the whole zone.
avoid: A kitchen island — the same clearance math as a standalone kitchen this size applies here.

hard_rules: A peninsula (not a full island) can define the kitchen edge while keeping the dining and living zones visually connected.
space_saving_tips: Rug boundaries separate the living zone from the dining/kitchen run without adding walls or bulk.
avoid: Uniform lighting across the whole zone — distinct lighting temperature per function is what actually makes an open plan read as zoned.

hard_rules: A full dining table (4–6 seats), a small kitchen island or peninsula, and a proper living seating cluster all coexist if each keeps its own clearance envelope.
space_saving_tips: A sofa back facing the dining zone acts as a soft divider without blocking sightlines.
avoid: Letting the kitchen work triangle bleed into the main walking path between the entry and the living zone.

hard_rules: Three fully distinct zones (cook, dine, lounge) each get real furniture commitments, with sightline management (Neufert §12) across all three becoming the main design constraint.
space_saving_tips: An island with seating on one side reduces the need for a fully separate breakfast nook.
avoid: Symmetric furniture placement that ignores which zone people actually enter from first.

hard_rules: Full-scale zoning (cook, dine, lounge, plus a possible fourth zone) is appropriate, but every zone boundary still needs a real circulation lane, not just implied furniture gaps.
space_saving_tips: A furniture 'spine' (console, bench, or low shelving run) organizes circulation between zones the way a hallway would in a compartmentalized plan.
avoid: Treating the extra space as a buffer instead of a zone — every square meter should belong to a function or it reads as unresolved.

hard_rules: A fold-down wall desk is the realistic ceiling if this room shares another primary function; a full stationary desk plus a visitor chair will not both fit.
space_saving_tips: Vertical cable management and a wall-mounted monitor arm reclaim desk depth.
avoid: A visitor/guest chair as a fixed piece — bring in a stool from another room only when needed.

hard_rules: A compact desk (100–110cm) fits with an ergonomic chair, but there's no room for a secondary seating or meeting element.
space_saving_tips: Wall-mounted shelving above the desk instead of a floor-standing bookshelf.
avoid: Facing the desk toward a blank wall if the room has a window — daylight orientation affects focus more than most other layout choices at this size.

hard_rules: A desk (120cm) plus ergonomic chair and a slim storage unit all fit within standard clearance.
space_saving_tips: A rolling file cart tucks under the desk when not in use instead of a permanent filing cabinet.
avoid: Placing the desk in the room's dead center 'for symmetry' — against a wall with a window view supports focus better and frees circulation.

hard_rules: A full desk, proper storage/bookshelf, and a small secondary seat (for calls or reading) all fit with room to spare.
space_saving_tips: A credenza behind the desk doubles as extra work surface and storage.
avoid: An oversized desk that doesn't match actual work needs — bigger isn't always more functional, and it eats into flexibility.

hard_rules: An L-shaped desk or a dual-zone setup (focus desk + casual reading corner) both work at this size.
space_saving_tips: A bookshelf-back room divider separates 'deep work' from 'call/meeting' zones within the same room.
avoid: Filling the extra footprint with decorative furniture unrelated to work function — it dilutes the room's primary purpose.

hard_rules: A full executive layout (desk, meeting nook, storage wall, reading chair) is justified, but each zone still needs its own clearance, same as any other room at this size.
space_saving_tips: A furniture spine or rug boundary keeps 'focus' and 'meeting' zones from blurring into one undifferentiated space.
avoid: Treating a large home office as license to add non-work furniture that competes with the room's primary function.
